Tianping Mountain, southwest of the old city of Suzhou, is where the family roots of Fan Zhongyan, a celebrated worthy of Wuzhong in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), lie. On the southern slope of Tianping Mountain are 121 ancient Ming-dynasty (1368–1644 CE) Chinese sweetgums over 420 years old, planted during the Wanli reign of the Ming by Fan Yunlin, a 17th-generation descendant of Fan Zhongyan; they are the same age as Tianping Mountain Villa, a representative late-Ming Jiangnan mountain garden. Since the 1980s, the Tianping Mountain Scenic Area has held a Red Maple Festival, and going to Tianping Mountain to admire the maples has become a must-do autumn activity for many Suzhou residents. This is the largest group of ancient Chinese sweetgums in East China; when temperatures fall, the net chlorophyll content drops, and during the color-change period the sweetgum leaves pass through three stages: green, yellow, and red.
Since field surveys began in 2022, every year at the end of October volunteers have had to keep pace with actual conditions; to photograph the ancient sweetgums when the whole forest is dyed, they ask daily, 'Have the sweetgums on Tianping Mountain turned red yet?' On October 24, 2023, we received a report from a journalist with the column 'The King Sends Him to Patrol the Mountain' from the front: 'A few trees have turned red; overall they haven't, and although the trees aren't fully red, the surging crowds are already in place!' Everyone joked: 'Waiting for plants to change color is like waiting for bananas to ripen—there's always a process. When viewing color-changing trees, at first you look for the multicolored display; if they all turned red at once, it would actually take away some of the fun of autumn viewing.' What is beyond doubt is that, under the anticipation of countless Suzhou residents, the ancient sweetgums always meet us once a year, keeping their appointment on schedule.

Driving onto Yinshan Island, between water and sky, one suddenly sees an ancient camphor standing tall, giving one the feeling of a lone tree keeping watch. For a very long period in the past, Yinshan Island hung in the middle of the lake with a sparse population; the ancient camphor was the representative of the island's lush vitality and could well be called the little island's guardian spirit. Local villagers say this tree was planted in the Tianji 4th year of Sun Hao of the Wu state during the Three Kingdoms period, more than 1,800 years ago, but judging by the current tree-age survey results, this legend can clearly only serve as mealtime conversation.
The ancient camphor's trunk is extremely massive; every time the volunteers went to Yinshan for field surveys, they could see tourists joining hands in a ring around the tree, trying to find out how many people it takes to embrace this ancient camphor with a circumference of 5.83 meters. A thousand-year-old camphor needs more room to grow, and the island's original residents are also glad to create good living conditions for the ancient camphor, and hung a 'Ancient Camphor Discussion Point' sign on its trunk, representing that this ancient camphor has become a public space for the villagers.

edits.find: Xishan is a paradise for ancient camphor trees, and there is even a scenic spot named after the camphor: the Ancient Camphor Garden, situated at the eastern foot of the Xishan hills. A Song cypress and a Yuan cypress stand there, the two trees forming a grove, lush and green. When time returns to the 1990s, the area around the Ancient Camphor Garden was still an unremarkable warehouse district. The villagers of Houbao Village could not bear to see such a place of outstanding natural beauty go to waste, so they raised funds to renovate the buildings in this area. A stele stands at the mountain gate of the Ancient Camphor Garden, erected after Houbao Village renovated the garden in 1995; it records that the site of the Ancient Camphor Garden 'supplied Guanyin in the Song and sacrificed to the City God in the Qing.' Both camphor trees long coexisted with the Guanyin Temple, the City God Temple, and other temples; in ancient times, temples such as the Guanyin Temple were themselves public spaces, serving to entertain the masses and to provide moral instruction. Here the ancient camphors played a role in which the ancient temple and the ancient trees complemented each other; on the other hand, because of their great height and other factors, the camphors could only be planted in open places, and in this way the camphor trees could functionally serve the public. Many temples and Daoist monasteries in Suzhou held temple fairs, markets, and similar activities, and the camphor trees themselves thus became markers of public space.

edits.find: For a long period, Mingyue Bay on West Hill drew the attention of the world. The Suzhou Prefecture Gazetteer records that this was "the place where the King of Wu enjoyed the moon," hence the name Mingyue Bay. But judging from the documents currently visible, Mingyue Bay probably began to win the favor of literati around the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE). Bai Juyi, Prefect of Suzhou, often went boating on Lake Tai, and in a letter to a friend he expressed his love for the scenery at the dock-head of Mingyue Bay: "Lake and hills everywhere are good for lingering; I love best the East Bay and the North Dock-head." About half a century later, torrential rains caused disaster in Suzhou. Pi Rixiu, then military judge of Suzhou, and his friend Lu Guimeng went to Linwu Cave on West Hill to sacrifice to the water god, and took the opportunity to tour all the famous sites of West Hill, each leaving behind a poem on the same topic, "Mingyue Bay." Yet whether Bai Juyi or Lu and Pi, their fame at Mingyue Bay fell far short of another Tang poet, Liu Changqing—and all because of a tree. In his poem "Seeking He Jiu at Mingyue Bay but Not Finding Him," Liu Changqing records that he traveled to West Hill to visit a friend: "The old friend is absent, the bright moon is here; who has seen the lone boat come and go?" Legend has it that after failing to find his friend, Liu Changqing could not bear his melancholy and planted a camphor tree. This camphor tree has weathered more than a thousand years and has been preserved to this day. The story appears in no other document, and may be simply a beautiful legend.

Mr. Huang: The name of Mingyue Bay Ancient Village comes from King Fuchai of Wu and Xi Shi coming here to enjoy the moon during the Spring and Autumn period. This ancient camphor is called by locals the Longevity Tree and the Immortal Tree. The tree was once burned. There are saw marks on its roots. Its 1,200-year history is like a museum. Its shape is like a grandfather carrying his grandson on his back. Its shade is especially cool.
Volunteer Luo Xinglin: I hear you always sit beside the ancient camphor, guarding this tree. Is there a story behind that?
Mr. Huang: In 1939, Japanese invaders went all over West Hill cutting trees. A local tyrant of West Hill brought people to Mingyue Bay to saw down the ancient camphor. The villagers could only pool money to avert disaster, and some elderly people even knelt and pleaded, so the order to stop sawing was barely given. The saw marks left then are still there today. In 1940, a band of bandits rushed into Mingyue Bay and insisted on cutting the tree. The villagers rose up in opposition. Seeing they could not get their way for the moment, the bandits took advantage of people's inattention and kidnapped me, then only ten years old, from Mingyue Bay to Zhejiang. Only after 36 days did the villagers manage to collect 120 shi of rice and redeem me from the bandits. Later, I felt I had a responsibility to protect this tree. For decades, rain or shine, I have only felt at ease guarding beside this tree.
While being interviewed, Mr. Huang saw a passing tour group of elderly visitors. He warmly encouraged the elderly tourists to touch the sacred tree with both hands, mentioning several times that the Qianlong emperor (reigned 1735–1796) had also touched it, and wishing everyone peace and long life.

Following the broad, level path through Luohan Hollow for some dozens of paces, one comes upon another stone-carved archway. Inscribed on its architrave in clerical script are the words "Ancient Luohan Temple," written by the Republic-era scholar Li Genyuan when he visited Xishan in 1929. On either side hangs a couplet composed by Shen Bingchun: "The wind makes melody of Buddhist chants; an ancient tree's path leads to quiet seclusion." Before seeing the tree, one already grasps its meaning. The wondrous sight of the wisteria and camphor intertwined stands before Luohan Temple. Two ancient camphor trees have known six hundred years of blooming; their crowns rise above the surrounding grove, their branches and leaves lush, their deep shade blotting out the sun. Around the trunk of one of these camphor trees coils a three-hundred-year-old Chinese wisteria, its vines winding upward along the camphor's trunk as if rushing into the clouds.
On April 15, 2023, when volunteers came according to the wisteria's blooming season in the city, they could see only a few flower buds high up on the ancient wisteria deep in the mountain hollow. Everyone wondered: could it be that the wisteria has decided not to bloom this year? An uncle who volunteers at Luohan Temple told us that temperatures in the mountains are lower, the ancient tree's crown blocks the sun, and the ancient tree near the ground gets little sunlight, so every year its blooming season comes later than in the city; we might as well come back a week later.
To photograph the wisteria and camphor at the peak of their intertwining, on April 23, 2023, everyone drove again to Jinting Town. How to describe the tree-viewing experience that day? One volunteer recalled that this was the most spectacular ancient tree encountered since the field survey began: the wisteria seen from the drone's viewpoint clung to the tree and climbed, like a purple waterfall hanging down, like stars of the Milky Way studding the sky; sitting or lying beneath it, one could well forget the world.

edits.find: In 1974, the former Chefang Commune of Wu County enclosed the lake to reclaim farmland on the western shore of Cheng Lake. After the lake water was pumped dry, a large number of ancient wells were discovered on the lakebed, and a great quantity of cultural relics was unearthed, among them the black-pottery jar with incised symbols and tubular handles displayed in the “Archaeology Explores Wuzhong” exhibition hall. This site lies today in Chengdun Village and Dayao Village on the western side of Cheng Lake in Luzhi Town; it was originally “Yaocheng,” a fief of the Spring and Autumn period (770–476 BCE), and the natural village “Dongjieshang” in the southeastern corner of Chengdun Village was in ancient times the market street of Yaocheng. Not far away, Dajue Temple Bridge was first built in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE) and rebuilt in the 11th year of the Zhizheng reign era of the Yuan dynasty (1351 CE); its body bears rare and exquisite carvings, and 60 meters to its east stands a Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Xianghua Bridge. Dajue Temple no longer exists; only the two ancient ginkgo trees on the site remain, standing apart from the world, holding out against the vast torrent of time.

edits.find: Driving into Dongshan Town in autumn, you need not seek it out deliberately to take in the boundless scenery of this 'home of ginkgo': ginkgos are planted everywhere—in the fields, by the lakeshore, in front of and behind houses—glowing with color. In villages such as Huwan, Guangming, Yangwan, Shangwan, Chawan and Baisha there are ancient ginkgos more than 500 years old. The tree with the longest registered age in Suzhou is hidden in Wanglingxia Village, Beiwang Ridge, Dongshan Town; if its 2,000-year age is accurate, then it was planted as far back as the Western Han. Villagers regard it as a 'sacred tree,' setting up an offering table beside it and building a small niche, where incense is kept burning year-round. The ancient tree's nameplate is wrapped around a slender new shoot; judging only from a photograph, one would mistake it for a young sapling. In fact, that is just one of the many suckering branches at the base of the trunk: after being struck by lightning, only a quarter of its trunk remained, yet dense new shoots sprouted from the roots. Long before humans appeared, the 'living fossil' ginkgo had already existed in the world for hundreds of millions of years. Its powerful capacity for self-healing and renewal is one of the secrets of this species' enduring survival.

During his residence in Suzhou from 1923 to 1937, Mr. Li Genyuan, a veteran of the Republican era, traveled throughout the western hills of Wu Commandery conducting antiquarian research and collecting and organizing a great deal of local historical material. Auntie Pingping is now over sixty; her grandfather, during his lifetime, planted several dozen hairy chestnut trees on Biluo Peak, and by reckoning of time these trees may already have passed the age threshold that defines an ancient tree.
She recalled that in those years her grandfather and granduncle planted several dozen trees on Biluo Peak; later, because of inadequate care, many had been cut down, leaving only some Chinese chestnuts, loquats, and orange trees mixed with tea on the hillside. After the interview ended, we suggested to her that we take a group photo of her with the chestnut trees her grandfather had planted. She smiled and lowered her head, one hand touching the tree and the other holding the tea leaves she had just picked, and said to us: "If you ever have the chance, please help speak up about the ancient trees too."

edits.find: Wintersweet (Chimonanthus praecox) gets its name because its fragrance resembles that of plum and its color resembles wax. The ancients once confused wintersweet with plum blossom, until the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE), when Fan Chengda, who lived at Shihu in Suzhou, clearly pointed out in his Fan Village Plum Manual that wintersweet is not a plum: "Wintersweet is originally not of the plum kind; because it blooms at the same time as plum, its fragrance is also similar, and its color entirely resembles a honeycomb, it is so named." He also divided it into three categories according to flower form: "There are in all three kinds. Those grown from seed and never grafted have small flowers and faint fragrance and rank lowest; they are called Jiuying Mei, popularly corrupted to Gousheng Mei. Those that have been grafted and whose flowers are half-open are called Jingkou Mei. Those deep yellow like red sandalwood and especially strongly fragrant are called Tanxiang Mei; this kind is the best." In recent decades, wintersweet has been cultivated in courtyards, gardens, and parks throughout Suzhou, flowering in early January each year.

edits.find:
Mingshan Hall
Mingshan Hall is located in the ancient village of Yangwan in Dongshan and is listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level. It consists mainly of a brick-carved gatehouse, a main hall, a flower hall, and a Buddhist tower. Its main hall is an early residential hall of the late Ming (1368–1644 CE) to early Qing (1644–1912 CE) period of exceptionally high artistic quality. The brick-carved gatehouse and the main hall are solemn and orderly in form, models of Suzhou residential architecture. The details of its three carvings and painted decoration incorporate the owner's aesthetic tastes: in the brick-carved gatehouse, for example, the spaces between the architraves are filled with inlaid floral geometric patterns, and the sumeru pedestals bear motifs such as peony scrolls and lotus with mandarin ducks; in the main hall, flowers and birds are carved in the mountain-mist and beam-embracing clouds, and the painted decoration is adorned with flowers such as lotus and baoxiang blossoms. These highly distinctive decorative features echo faintly the small garden in front of the flower hall. The flower hall stands to the front left of the main hall; its front courtyard contains a small garden planted with wintersweet and camellia, while its rear courtyard is planted with Chinese boxwood—in contrast to the solemn, orderly ritual order of the main axis, it appears more lively. Residential buildings in the Wuzhong area seem mostly to have treated the main hall as a stern place for receiving guests and socializing, while the flower hall to one side was the more relaxed study or place for enjoying the garden; for example, the lacebark pine of Chunxi Hall in this exhibition is likewise in the small garden in front of a flower hall. Times have changed, yet we can still imagine the owner's elegant life in Mingshan Hall's flower hall: admiring camellia in spring, leaning by the boxwood in summer, and picking wintersweet in winter. So where is autumn? Dongshan has been a land of ginkgo since ancient times; the cool autumn wind will of course invite sheet after sheet of yellow leaves onto the owner's desk.

A century-old Chinese catalpa, numbered '吴中076', stands behind Mengjiang Hall in Xia Village, Yuwu, Group 5 of Biluo Village, Dongshan. The old tree is not easy to find, but Mengjiang Hall, which carries the faith of Dongshan's villagers, is known to everyone you ask. This small temple, three bays wide, is already a hundred years old, and its hall plaque reads 'Liu Fu Zhong Tian Wang' (Central Heavenly King of the Liu Estate). The catalpa is not inside the hall but in the courtyard of a Wang family household behind it. Curiously, two plaques for ancient and notable trees hang on the tree: one newly hung in 2018 identifies it as a Chinese catalpa, while the one from 2004 reads 'zicatalpa' (Catalpa ovata). Nearby villagers, including 89-year-old Wang Quanxing, who lives in the small courtyard with the old tree, firmly believe it is a zicatalpa.
The Book of Han says: 'The catalpa—there are also those who mistakenly call it zi.' Being mistaken for a zicatalpa is almost the fate of every old Chinese catalpa in Suzhou. Early records contain a note that 'there are eight zicatalpas in greater Suzhou', when in fact six of them are Chinese catalpas. Besides Dongshan in Wuzhong, the two old Chinese catalpas in front of Sanfeng Temple in Changshu also once bore plaques reading 'zicatalpa'; in 2015 He Wenyue, a member of the Changshu Peasants and Workers Party, submitted a 'Proposal on Reidentifying the Two Zicatalpas at Sanfeng Temple'. In 2018, Associate Professor Wang Jinhu of Suzhou University of Science and Technology went to the Suzhou Confucian Temple to admire the blossoms and judged from flower color and leaf shape that all three old trees bearing 'zicatalpa' plaques should be Chinese catalpas.
Chinese catalpa and zicatalpa are like a pair of similar twins. Both are trees of the genus Catalpa in the family Bignoniaceae, and both share the same virtues: fast growth, moderate hardness, light weight and wear resistance—fine timber. A folk saying runs, 'A thousand-year cypress, a ten-thousand-year fir, are no match for a single branch of catalpa.' In the Wuzhong Culture Museum's 'Archaeological Exploration of Wuzhong' gallery, the Warring States zither unearthed at Changqiao Village in Wuxian County was made of catalpa and maple wood; its body is hard in texture, and it is one of the earliest Spring and Autumn and Warring States zithers yet found in archaeological excavations.

This Dragon Juniper has now been removed from the official list of ancient and notable trees because it died. Its death is estimated to have occurred between 2017 and 2021. The 2017 edition of the Dongshan Town Gazetteer records that in 2013 most of the tree's branches suddenly died; after rescue efforts its growth recovered somewhat. Judging by the present outcome, those rescue efforts ultimately failed to save the ancient tree, which became an eternal regret.
The name Qilong Hall is connected to the locally circulated legend of Xu Qilong. According to the 2017 edition of the Dongshan Town Gazetteer, this building enshrines the fierce general bodhisattva, so it can also be understood as a fierce-general hall of the kind found in almost every village in Dongshan. The stone stele in front of the hall is the Ming Jiajing-era 'Wuxian 28th Du, 13th Tu Community' stele. According to the scholar Zhao Shiyu, it is powerful evidence that the Ming dynasty's community (lishe) system was implemented in Dongshan.
Today incense still burns continuously around the Dragon Juniper. It is said that villagers once invited a eminent monk to perform rites to help the withered tree recover, but parasitic plants around the ancient tree have long gone uncleared; vines cover it and young trees grow lushly, as if it had revived. Whether this is a withered tree coming back to life or a final flicker before death remains open to debate. In any case, perhaps this ancient tree can continue to shelter later generations after its death, achieving mutual fulfillment with this small temple submerged in the sea of history and with the ordinary yet devout villagers.

On the stone-slab path on the southeast side in front of the gate hall of Dunyu Hall stands a thousand-year-old Chinese wisteria. Zheng Yanshao's Qing-dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Continued Notes on Taihu records: "In the street before the hall there is one wisteria, stretching across several hundred paces; a trellis of timber supports it, great stones prop it, and iron ropes run through it. In flowering season the blossoms hang down like tassels, scattering fragrance over the ground; this place has become a market, and no one knows how many years it has been so. When this plant was set here, it surely was not in the marketplace; the ages of the great chun tree can hardly be reckoned. I once asked the elders, who said: 'From childhood to old age we have never seen it grow larger. Now several decades more have passed, and the trunk remains as before.' All things that neither wither nor flourish excessively attain long life; one may grasp this principle from it."
In April 2023, in the season when the wisteria blooms, volunteers from the Tree Stele and Biography project went to Dongshan Old Street to record this wisteria. They happened upon an 81-year-old neighborhood uncle, especially talkative, who recalled that about 30 years ago this wisteria had been rescued: when the borer holes in the main trunk grew large, they were sealed with material. Earlier, when utility lines were buried, in order not to harm the wisteria's roots, the pavement near the wisteria was not dug up; instead the original drainage pipe was borrowed, but that year the flowers bloomed less well than in previous years.
Mr. Ye, who lives next door to Dunyu Hall, warmly invited the volunteers up to his rooftop to view the wisteria and incidentally look down into the interior of Dunyu Hall. He explained that Dunyu Hall originally belonged to the Xi family of Dongshan and was about 150 meters deep; after Liberation most of it was divided up. The part now visible had once been a tea factory; after the tea factory moved away it stood empty, and after restoration it served for a time as a celebrity museum; after the museum moved a few years ago it has again stood empty to this day. The courtyard is overgrown with weeds, dead vines fill the spaces between the tiles, and ivy trails from the load-bearing columns all the way to the door lintel. The old man sighed that a house easily deteriorates once no one lives in it, and that the old buildings of Dunyu Hall were a pity. As we left, Mr. Ye could not help seeing us off, escorting us all the way to beneath the wisteria blossoms.

Before searching the map for this tree's coordinates, the volunteers knew nothing of the place name "Shuidongbang." One autumn, they drove there on the off chance, and sure enough, behind a house they saw a blaze of gold: a 600-year-old ginkgo. Although the surroundings are mostly orchards and farmland, beneath the tree are large characters reading "Dongbang," along with fitness equipment and chairs, making it veritably a new community center.
The other tree is much more slender and stands across the paddy fields. Bridge, temple, tree—this is the standard Jiangnan ancient-ginkgo configuration. Yangwan Village lies in the southwestern part of Dongshan Town. The natural villages along the lakeshore include Shangwan, Tunwan, Chengwan, Husha, Wanli and others; their names alone reveal the water-ringed topography here. Husha Temple is built on a hillside. The plaque above the temple gate reads "Hujie Tang Chaowang," and there are also the characters "Taihu Xinglong She"; a flag reading "Taihu Xinglong She" hangs there as well.
The name "Xinglong She" has appeared in Wujiang. Xia Yihong, one of the authors of *Chuihong Wensu: Modern and Contemporary Jiangnan Society and Culture in the Field*, did a case study of the Xinglong She at the Xu Family Gongmen Temple in Miaogang, Wujiang. Zhao Shiyu, author of *The General Returns Home: A New Jiangnan History of Dongting Dongshan*, believes they belong to the same system. The person in charge of Husha Temple is also surnamed Xu and indeed moved here from Wujiang. He also thinks the meaning of "Chaowang" may be related to Taihu fishermen's "Four Courts, North and South"—that is, Husha Tang may be a branch temple of one of the shrines in the "Four Courts." Some scholars have investigated the "Four Courts, North and South" of Wujiang fishermen as "the Southern Court: Liu Mengjiang at Liansidang, Jiaxing; the Northern Court: the Great Mother at Shangfang Mountain, Suzhou; the Eastern Court: Lord Yang at Jinze Town, Qingpu; the Western Court: the Three Great Lords at Shicong, Huzhou." Different parts of the Taihu region have different versions, but in any case these are spatial markers of the water world in fishermen's consciousness, similar to the Five Sacred Mountains and the Four Seas.
The ancient tree in front of the temple is a Chinese zelkova over 200 years old. In spring it puts forth captivating new green, guarding the village's peace together with the little temple. It has been observed that the tree has a very large hollow. The ancient-tree conservation worker Zhang Ji mentions that such a tree scar formed when disease or pests were not treated in time, and because rainwater flows back in, the hollow has grown larger and larger. Yet we can always trust the tree's capacity for self-healing: even a scar close to the diameter of the trunk at breast height can gradually be wrapped up by newly grown bark. Gazing at the twisted trunk, we seem able to imagine its struggles and perseverance over these hundred years.

From 2023 to 2024, volunteers visited several ancient Chinese zelkovas on Yushan Island in Dongshan and at Husha Temple and other places. Their colorful swaying in late autumn and their new green sprouting in late spring are both captivating, but what left the deepest impression on the volunteers were the huge hollows and scars on the trunks—wounds left by the years, yet all the more highlighting the ancient trees' powerful vitality.
Around "tree scars," the volunteers specially interviewed the ancient-tree conservation worker Zhang Ji.
Wang Mingyu, curator at the Wu Museum: Teacher Zhang, we found that these Chinese zelkovas all have some tree scars. How are they caused?
Zhang Ji: Scars on a tree are like scars on a human body. After breakage, tearing, mechanical damage and the like, the surviving part, in order to heal the wound, rapidly divides cells in the cambium at the damaged area and grows new tissue to protect itself, preventing harm from rain, pests and disease. Tree scars form different shapes depending on the wound. Because they are newly grown, they differ greatly in color and shape from the old bark, showing obvious scars on the tree body.
Volunteer Zhou Yuan: The two ancient trees on Yushan Island and at Husha Temple both healed through tenacious self-healing after being injured. What kind of mechanism is this?
Zhang Ji: Ancient trees are living organisms. When they suffer external damage, they show the ability to protect themselves and resist invasion from outside. The tree body relies on its bark to protect itself and to contact the outside world; this is a defensive barrier. Once the barrier is destroyed and cannot heal, the interior of the tree easily dies and forms a hollow. The variously shaped healed wounds we see on ancient trees are in fact expressions of their self-repair, and the wounds on ancient trees are often quite large, so it is a long process.

Volunteer Zhou Yuan: What artificial methods can we use to protect injured ancient trees?
Zhang Ji: Ancient trees have different kinds of wounds.
1. Some have large areas of bark damaged or missing. We can scrape the damaged edges clean with a sharp blade, clean and preserve the wood that lacks bark protection, and artificially provide a temporary protective barrier until the surrounding bark slowly grows and wraps around, healing the wound.
2. Some have large hollows or broken branches, especially wounds from torn branches. In such cases, we first clean the opening of the hollow or the break; dead wood must not protrude from the opening or extend beyond the living bark, because dead wood will hinder the wrapping and healing.
Wang Mingyu, curator at the Wu Museum: In the process of ancient-tree protection, are there any unforgettable stories you can share?
Zhang Ji: Actually, I think the process of ancient-tree protection is a kind of archaeology, especially when working on the underground part. The surface appearance of ancient trees today has been greatly changed by human activity, and many ancient-tree problems need to be solved underground. Unless you dig open the soil around the roots, you will never know the secrets buried below. And as ancient trees grow they send out signals; we must discover the signals in time and promptly investigate and resolve the problems, so that the ancient trees can extend their lives in the lives of our generation.
For example:
1. An ancient tree may for a long time have sparse branches and leaves, small leaves, an unhealthy color, and lack of vigor; sometimes one side of a tree is vigorous while the other side looks listless. If we dig open the soil on the listless side, we may find too many stones underground or the ruins of earlier buildings, which obstruct root growth and cause malnutrition.
2. The leaves may be half withered and yellow, half green, with gray-black between the yellow and green, and a large amount of fallen leaves may be seen under the tree. If we dig deep into the soil, we may see that the deep soil is very wet, the roots black or even foul-smelling, and sometimes we can find drainage ditches built by people in earlier years that, through long neglect or abandonment amid urban and rural construction, no longer drain the standing water, so the ancient tree lives uncomfortably here—and so it sends people signals.
3. Some ancient trees in the countryside have peculiar wounds on certain parts. According to oral accounts of nearby elders, in some cases many years ago, when this was a natural village, this was the place where cattle were tethered and raised; in others, near a river, it was where small boats moored and tied their cables.
4. Some ancient trees have roots that have wrapped around stone steles, Buddha statues, millstones and the like; some lean in front of old houses, giving the doorway a natural great umbrella; some stand quietly at the village entrance, letting you hang bells and paste wedding notices on them, quietly watching over each generation of the village as they come and go and finally return. Looking at the people at the village entrance who entrust their nostalgia to the ancient tree, I think this expresses a kind of harmony and inclusiveness between humans and nature.

The first field visit to this tree was in spring, and the volunteers present all marveled: a ginkgo in spring could actually be this beautiful. Most of the old streets and houses in Husha have been rebuilt in recent years; Liu Gong Tang, built in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), is one of the few surviving historic buildings, with two successive courtyards, and its gatehouse is three bays wide, built in the Qing dynasty. It once served as the office of the Overseas Chinese Cemetery; after repairs, a ceiling was installed and walls were built, and it is now abandoned.
The ginkgo in front of the gate is 500 years old. In 1956, the master of Chinese painting Li Keran sketched in Dongshan and left behind the work 'Suzhou's Thousand-Year Ginkgo,' which is probably this tree. While we were gathered around the tree discussing it, an Aunt Chen from the village passed by, said the ancient ginkgo belonged to her family, and warmly invited the volunteers to sit at her home; the ginkgo's canopy can be seen from her courtyard. In her parents' generation, several families raised and protected this ginkgo together. There is a government subsidy of two thousand yuan each year; generally fertilizer is applied once in autumn, and pests and diseases are promptly dealt with and reported, so its overall health is good, and caring for it has become part of several families' lives. Aunt Chen married into the Shi family of Husha from Duqiao decades ago and has of course benefited from the ginkgo; the fruit is also divided among three Shi households, 200 jin for the large household and 100 jin for the small ones. This grafted female ginkgo can harvest more than five hundred jin of ginkgo nuts a year; the nuts are small, the flesh round, green when shelled, and sweet in taste.

Banks' rose is often cultivated in gardens, climbing over trellises or walls and hedges, and is a common flower in Suzhou. Wen Zhenheng of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) records in Zhangwuzhi (Treatise on Superfluous Things): "I have often seen that in the gardens of households, bamboo is invariably used to make a screen, with five-colored roses drawn over it, and timber framed into a pavilion, called a Banks' rose trellis. When the flowers bloom, people sit beneath it promiscuously—how is this different from a tavern? Yet these two kinds cannot be planted without a screen or trellis; perhaps moving them to the women's quarters, for the ladies to pick, would be somewhat acceptable. Walking into the Master of the Nets Garden, visitors can easily spot a "bare tree" on the far side of Cangxia Pond. This unassuming-looking Chinese juniper is more than 900 years old and is said to have been planted by hand by Shi Zhizhi, a vice minister of the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) and the garden's first owner. The ancient juniper is about 10 meters tall, the "high point" around Cangxia Pond, and the oldest tree in Gusu District. More than 130 years ago, the garden's owner planted a lacebark pine beside it; today the pine and juniper stand shoulder to shoulder. "Pines and junipers are naturally solitary and upright, ill-suited to the faces of peach and plum"; compared with brief splendor, they have chosen enduring resilience.
People who observe trees over the long term pay attention not only to the changes of the four seasons but are drawn even more to distinctive tree forms. The volunteers of the Tree Stele project jokingly consider Wang 003 a tree with personality: its lower trunk is tall and straight, and the juniper foliage at the top grows sparser with age, yet its branches and trunk are like a person dancing for joy, retaining vigorous vitality. Searching through Wu-school painting and calligraphy, we find that Wen Zhengming's 'Cunju Tu' (Painting of Preserved Chrysanthemums) also depicts a tree with personality. Comparing the forms of the branches, we cannot help wondering: might the literati of the Wu school of painting also have noticed this ancient juniper?

The crape myrtle has a long history of cultivation in Suzhou. It is also called wei hua ("wei flower") and is named after the Ziwei star. Little known is that "Ziwei lang" ("Gentleman of the Ziwei Star") was another name for a Secretariat Drafter; the playful self-mockery in the line "Ashamed all day long to face you, for I am no Ziwei lang" captures the fondness for the crape myrtle among the great and powerful of successive dynasties.
Wen Zhenheng of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) records in Zhang Wu Zhi (Treatise on Superfluous Things): "There are four kinds of wei flower: besides the purple, the white is called white wei, the red is called red wei, and the purple with a touch of blue is called emerald wei." The crape myrtle has a long flowering period and is an important summer flowering plant. Zhang Wu Zhi also says: "This flower opens in the fourth month and fades in the ninth; commonly called 'Hundred-Day Red.' Planted in a mountain garden, it may be called a 'friend that endures.'" The one in the Garden of Harmony is a rare "Silver Crape Myrtle": not a vivid purplish red but a plain, clean white, adding further refinement.
Suzhou's gardens are not short of ancient crape myrtles either, though unfortunately each has more or less a flaw: the 640-year-old crape myrtle in the Garden of Harmony is said to have been planted by the top scholar Wu Kuan; its main trunk has now died, leaving only one side branch cautiously continuing the literary line—the trunk withered, the flowers blooming as before, and even reaching out beyond the wall, presenting different views inside and outside the moon gate. The Garden of Harmony was built on the site of the old residence of Wu Kuan, a Ming-dynasty top scholar of Suzhou, and tradition says the ancient tree was planted by Wu Kuan himself, earning it the name "Top Scholar's Crape Myrtle." Counting back the years and consulting the literature, this claim is not accurate; however, Wu Kuan was quite interested in plants, and after going to the capital to serve as an official he often missed the common plants of Jiangnan, writing a long essay as a record of them.

In today's old city of Suzhou there are still many small lanes that electronic maps have never explored. Following the vague wording "Xinsuili, Donghai Island" in the gazetteers, we wandered round and round the narrow alleys until at last, through a gap between clothes-drying poles and electric wires, we glimpsed a tree in all its splendor. Legend says the ancient tree was "planted by Zhang Shicheng at the end of the Yuan dynasty," but 540 years ago was the Chenghua era of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), so this claim is easy to disprove. Yet the legend of its being "planted by Zhang Shicheng" is not without reason: not far from the ancient ginkgo is a lane called "Chengtian Temple Front." When Zhang Shicheng held Suzhou, he first occupied Chengtian Temple and built the East and West Travel Palaces; because these two palaces were woven with waterways and seemed impregnable as metal walls and boiling moats, the place names "Donghai Island" and "Xihai Island" have been passed down to this day, and only then did this ancient ginkgo—younger than Zhang Shicheng—become its friend across the generations.
Today all kinds of mops hang from its thick trunk; residents loll about in twos and threes on bamboo chairs beneath the tree, chatting; now and then an auntie draws water from the well; little children run about cheering for the falling ginkgo leaves, as if this tree had become an inseparable member of the big family. It is so tall, yet hides its greatness in the city; it is so ancient, yet fits so naturally into the life of ordinary lanes.

On the route from Beisita Metro Station to the Humble Administrator's Garden, if you look from Xibei Street toward Tingyuan Road, you can see that this road has made a small roundabout for a tree. A camphor tree stands at a slant in the center, its branches and leaves lush, huge as an umbrella.
An ancient tree occupying a good location has witnessed the vicissitudes of several hundred years. Its site was originally the residence of the Zhang family of the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE), who later donated the house to become a temple. During the Jiajing reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), Fujian merchants, following the example of the Tianfei Palace in Taicang, also built a Tianhou Palace in Suzhou dedicated to Mazu, and chose this site. The Wu Men Biao Yin records: "On the stone archway at the gate of the Tianhou Palace, to the left and right are carved sixteen characters: 'The gods are near; each should be reverent; officials, soldiers, and common people, dismount here.' Over the past century or so, the Tianhou Palace has successively been used by Beijie Central Primary School, the Municipal No. 38 Middle School, a vocational middle school, and the No. 3 Middle School branch campus; today it has been developed into a villa area. The ancient camphor tree is precisely the survivor of the two camphor trees that once stood before the main hall of the Tianhou Palace. When the road was built at the beginning of this century, between building a straight road and making a detour to protect the tree, the people of Suzhou chose the latter. A city willing to yield the road to a tree—that is some foresight, and no little deep feeling.

The Suzhou Prefectural School Confucian Temple was first built in the second year of the Jingyou reign of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), in 1035 CE. Today, many ancient trees can still be found in the Confucian Temple. Six weather-beaten ginkgos stand guard on the south side of the Dacheng Hall. The one on the west, numbered '沧501,' was planted in the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) and is more than 800 years old; it is called the 'Longevity Ginkgo' (Shouxing). Because it was once struck by lightning, only half its trunk remains, leaning slightly. The 600-year-old 'Intertwined Ginkgo' (Lianli Xing) was also struck by lightning, and remarkably, a Chinese hackberry and a Chinese catalpa grew out of its hollow interior, embracing as one body—hence its name. The 'Three Firsts Ginkgo' (Sanyuan Xing) was completely destroyed by lightning in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE); when Qian Qi, a student at the Suzhou Prefectural School, successively placed first in the provincial, metropolitan, and palace examinations, new shoots grew from the old root in three forks, and the world called it the 'Three Firsts Ginkgo.'
Four hundred years ago, the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) Wumen painter Qian Gong depicted a scene in the south of Suzhou, including the Lingxing Gate and Dacheng Hall of today's Confucian Temple; the architectural form and layout are little different from today, with ancient trees standing in groves before the Dacheng Hall, among them three ginkgos that have grown to the present day.
Since the nineteenth century, photography has only recently entered China. The Dacheng Hall of the Suzhou Confucian Temple, with its rich heritage and grand architectural form, attracted many Chinese and foreign photographers to stop and photograph. Looking through old black-and-white photographs, the earliest images of these ancient trees date back to 1889: the Dacheng Hall photographed by the Norwegian explorer Carl Bock, probably a winter scene, with the Longevity Ginkgo and the Intertwined Ginkgo in the front courtyard both bare-branched; the setting sun stretched the Longevity Ginkgo's shadow very long. What is moving is that this moment of sparse vegetation is only one several-hundredth of its long years; in the following year, the cycle repeats, and the ginkgos before the hall will continue to sprout until the vegetation is lush.
The Confucian Temple continues Suzhou's thousand-year cultural lineage. As one of the main ancient buildings in the central urban area, politicians, scholars, and tourists visiting Suzhou come in droves, and in the old images they took, we see the ancient trees guarding the Dacheng Hall face to face, year after year, just the same.

Inside Suzhou No. 100 Hospital stands a seven-hole granite beam bridge called the Jiecao Nunnery Stone Bridge. This site was originally Dayun Nunnery, founded in the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE) and also known as Jiecao Nunnery; it was rebuilt several times in the Ming (1368–1644 CE) and Qing (1644–1912 CE) dynasties. Today its halls and stone pagoda are all destroyed, yet the square life-release pond has been preserved, and the form of this stone bridge is likewise a unique example within the old city of Suzhou.
Standing here together with the stone bridge is an ancient lacebark pine roughly 220 years old. This place may have been a paradise for ancient lacebark pines. In the tenth year of the Hongzhi reign of the Ming (1497), Shen Zhou spent the night at Dayun Nunnery and later painted the 'Record of a Visit to the Thatched Nunnery' (Caolan Jiyou Tu). Through the 'Poems Recording a Visit to the Thatched Nunnery' (Caolan Jiyou Shi) and the painting and calligraphy, the layout of Dayun Nunnery can still be reconstructed: 'In the quarters of the abbot, Master Mao, situated in the east side, there is a Buddha hall; behind it stretches an earthen ridge some forty zhang long and over three zhang high, on which stands an ancient gua, towering ten xun, its branches crooked and deeply green—a thing of several hundred years.' 'Gua' means the lacebark pine. In the upper-left corner of the painting we can clearly see that the simply outlined trunk bears mottled, scaly bark, a typical feature of the lacebark pine. Although the age of this ancient lacebark pine, 沧529, does not match the Ming dynasty of more than four hundred years ago, just like Canglang Pavilion next door to No. 100 Hospital—'Today at Canglang, ask not who is master; a hundred years of rise and fall are but the same waves'—the ancient tree and the ancient architectural remains pass the baton onward, wave after wave, intermittently yet completely bearing witness to the succession of the years.

As the only ancient yulan magnolia in the old city, "沧553" has stood at the Former Site of the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commission for more than three hundred years. As early as the early Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), this place was the provincial water conservancy sub-office; in the fourteenth year of the Hongzhi reign (1501), it was changed to a surveillance sub-office, and later it handled military preparedness affairs exclusively and was called the "Military Preparedness Circuit"—which is how the road name "Daoqian Street" came about. In the eighth year of the Yongzheng reign of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), that is 1730, the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commissioner moved from Jiangning to Suzhou, and the Military Preparedness Circuit office was changed into the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner's yamen, which was in charge of judicial and penal affairs in the province. In the sixth year of the Tongzhi reign of the Qing dynasty, that is 1867, Governor Guo Boyin rebuilt this place; during the Republican period it was changed into the Jiangsu High Court. For more than three hundred years, this ancient tree has witnessed changes in the administrative functions of the ancient buildings.
Observing and recording ancient and notable trees has never been work that can be completed in a single year; for two consecutive years, the volunteers of Tree Steles and Biographies visited this place. In March 2023, because the ancient buildings at the Former Site of the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commission, a provincial-level protected site, were being restored, scaffolding was put up in the courtyard; in this, one of her more than three hundred bloomings, she kept company with the scaffolding and the construction workers. In March 2024, the restoration of the ancient buildings was completed and the former site reopened to the public; the ancient tree still bloomed in spring with vigorous vitality.
In ancient times the purple magnolia was called Xinyi or Mubi; the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) painter Shen Zhou painted the handscroll Xinyi and Ink Cabbage. This tree is recorded in the register as "Purple Magnolia," but judging from its characteristics, it is more likely a Erqiao Magnolia. The purple magnolia and the Erqiao Magnolia have similar flower shapes and close flower colors, and sometimes the two are hard to distinguish. The Erqiao Magnolia is a hybrid of the yulan magnolia and the purple magnolia; it inherits the flower color of the purple magnolia and the tree habit of the yulan magnolia, and its tree form is slightly smaller than that of the yulan magnolia—it is a small tree that flowers before leafing out and has nine petals. The purple magnolia has a late flowering period; it is a low shrub that flowers and leafs out at the same time, its outermost whorl of tepals is reduced to narrow sepal-like structures, and its inner whorl has six tepals.

At the 'Office for Educational Equipment and Work-Study Management' at No. 13 Yingfengqiao Lane, through the fence at the entrance, we can see an unremarkable Chinese red-bean tree. It is not beautiful; in spring and autumn it is bare, and only in early summer does it put out new branches. Yet across the whole of southern Jiangsu only about ten ancient red-bean trees survive, and this 360-year-old Ming-dynasty red-bean tree is the oldest one inside the old city—extremely rare. 'No. 13 Yingfengqiao Lane' is not an area open to the public, but the red-bean tree is famous far and wide, and when asked about it, the elderly people nearby and the guard at the gate will recite the line 'May you gather more of them; this thing best stirs longing.'
The red-bean tree originally belonged to No. 37 Wuyachang, in the former residence of Wu Zhijia, a Ming-dynasty Suzhou native and Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice. The street name 'Wuyachang' comes precisely from him. In the history books there are only a few brief lines about Wu Zhijia: he was caught up in the protracted 'Contest over the Heir Apparent' during the Wanli reign, and he, Wu Yuanjia of Changzhou, Ye Chunchu of Wuxian, and Zhang Dong of Kunshan were all censured and sent home, known at the time as the 'Three Remonstrators of Wu.' In one lifetime he left behind an alley, a red-bean tree, and a line in the history books—enough, one might say, to have 'not failed the world of men.'

Sanjiaojing Ginkgo Square stands at the junction of two main roads, Liuhong Road and Zhongshan Road. It is the site of Shengshou Chan Temple and was once the city center of Wujiang; today only a single ginkgo remains, which happens to stand behind a bus stop, and because of this the stop is praised by locals as the 'Ginkgo Station.' Legend has it that Sanjiaojing was built by Wu Shan, a man of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE). In his post at the Ministry of Justice he carefully examined the records of prisoners' crimes and overturned more than a hundred doubtful cases; Sanjiaojing is therefore also tangible evidence of Wu Shan's treating others with virtue.
As the urban area of Wujiang expanded, Shengshou Chan Temple long ago disappeared, and naturally no one inquired after Sanjiaojing either; and with the outward relocation of modern commerce, the square no longer performs its original function, yet it remains an important landmark in people's hearts. Sanjiaojing, the ginkgo and the square have, since their birth, benefited from this city's prosperity and development; after the passing of white clouds and the transformations of seas and mulberry fields, the surroundings may be vastly different, and so they step forward once more to bear counter-evidence to that distant yet still vivid era. They are time, they are the years, they are history, and still more they are witness, spirit and eternity.

According to the Wujiang Archives, Yuantong Temple was formerly Yuantong Nunnery. The earliest record of Yuantong Nunnery appears in the Continued Gazetteer of Wujiang County from the Kangxi reign: "Yuantong Nunnery is at Hupu; it was built by the monk Songyin in the first year of the Tianqi reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE)." By modern times, only two old ginkgo trees and a few dilapidated buildings remained of Yuantong Nunnery. Because more than ten other kinds of plants grow as epiphytes on one of the ginkgos, it has the alternative name "Ten Scenes."
Temples were sometimes called "chanlin" (monastery groves), and ginkgo was customarily used in place of the bodhi tree. The ginkgo also happens to be a long-lived species, so in Jiangnan settlements the companion of an old ginkgo is very likely an old temple; this seems almost a fixed pattern. Nearly every settlement crossed by a river once had such a scene: on the first and fifteenth of each lunar month, barefoot children would clutch candles and go flitting unsteadily across a ramshackle yet solid old bridge; as soon as they reached the ginkgo, the sound of sutra chanting from the old temple would swirl around their ears. Half understanding, they would hand their candles to a grandmother in a flowered headscarf, her face flickering in and out of view in the light filtered through the ginkgo leaves, as devout and sacred as the incense burning in the censer.

Mr. Chen Congzhou held that the lacebark pine "stands alone in Chinese gardens." With its twisting, dragon-like form and its immortal white color, it is indeed a landscape tree of exceptional ornamental value. Compared with the stout, burly ancient lacebark pines of Beihai's Round City and Jietai Temple in Beijing, the lacebark pines in Suzhou gardens often appear crooked. Suzhou people call this "mentou" ("muffled head"): while the tree is still small, the main branch is cut off, and the branches may then spread at a slant. I believe the main reason for this north-south difference is the difference in architectural purpose. Whether it is the "White-Robed General" or the "Nine-Dragon Pine," both create a sense of stern order, whereas most Suzhou lacebark pines appear in private gardens, accompanied by lake rocks, winding bridges, and flowing water, presenting a literati painterly mood.
Guo Xi, a painting theorist of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), held that "water should seem distant; if it is fully shown, it is not distant; if it is screened and its flow interrupted, then it is distant." Joseph Needham held that "generally speaking, distance in Chinese painting is expressed by height; usually objects placed behind are painted higher than those in front, but not necessarily smaller, which gives many Chinese paintings the character of a bird's-eye view, all objects seeming to be seen from a certain height." That building is the Liu residence known as Shuxuan Tang, which originally had no connection with Wumengtang; one must contact the administrator to find the key before entering. Only by visiting both places can one fully grasp the story of this ancient wintersweet.
When wintersweet is mentioned, Chao Buzhi contributed its most famous literary anecdote: "Its fragrance is faint and its bearing plain, / I recall Su'er, just like this plum"—using his friend's maidservant Su'er as a metaphor for wintersweet to create a celebrated line. From then on, Su'er became another name for wintersweet.
Yejia Dai in Beishe, Wujiang, has the oldest wintersweet in the whole Suzhou municipality. Wintersweets are inherently hard-pressed to live long, and this one also marks a brilliant literary coordinate—Wumengtang. The Ye family of Wumengtang was a famous literary clan in Wujiang's history: Ye Shaoyuan and his wife Shen Yixiu, together with their seven sons and four daughters, who were steeped in their parents' influence, were all rich in literary thought and talent, producing a great quantity of poetry and prose, collected in the Collected Works of Wumengtang (Wumengtang Ji).
Among them the best known member is surely Ye Xiaoluan. Folk legend says that although Ye Xiaoluan was born into the Ye family, where literary culture flourished, in her childhood she was for some reason raised by her maternal aunt, who fortunately was likewise a beauty of both talent and learning and devoted herself to teaching Ye Xiaoluan. Later Ye Xiaoluan returned to the Ye family and planted a wintersweet in front of Shuying Tower to commemorate her aunt's nurturing kindness; thereafter she produced a great many works and enjoyed some renown in the literary world of the time. Yet heaven envied her talent: Ye Xiaoluan, deeply cherished by her parents, sadly died of illness before her marriage. As if struck by this blow, and with the times in turmoil, the Ye family gradually declined thereafter. Folk tradition therefore once widely held that Ye Xiaoluan was the prototype for Lin Daiyu in Dream of the Red Chamber.
This legend has circulated for a long time, but many details remain hard to verify. It has no dramatic twists and turns; everyone is full of truth, goodness, and beauty, as in an ideal realm, yet it ends with a cruel twist of fate, as if witnessing the collapse of an ivory tower. I believe the legend of Wumengtang is so widely told not only because of the scholarly standing of the Collected Works of Wumengtang, but also because it embodies the general public's admiration for the Ye family's atmosphere, their regret over the talented beauty Ye Xiaoluan's ill fate, and their grief over a literary heaven crumbling overnight. The family environment Ye Shaoyuan created had a modernity that transcended its era: elders and young in harmony, no distinction between sons and daughters, masters and servants close to one another. "Dabei Nunnery" is another fairly common name for a community temple. If we could get into the halls to observe, many things would be readily resolved—yet once again we were met with a closed door.
Fortunately, this is a place where temple-and-bridge culture is strikingly at work. The Yangjia Bridge beside it is also called Huiyuan Bridge; "Huiyuan" ("confluence of sources") can sometimes also be understood as a kind of water-deity worship—where river sources meet, the currents surge and race, so naturally the waters again need to be subdued. Judging by the geographical setting, the rivers on both the east and west sides of Yangjia Bridge become broad, making bridge-building inconvenient; this kind of hydrological feature is popularly called a "gourd pocket" (huludou). Thus Yangjia Bridge, which grips the neck of the gourd pocket, became a transport hub. Because temples need believers, they often choose sites where people are dense, and they also like to plant ginkgos—so many ancient ginkgos in Wujiang stand at bridgeheads. Often, finding a tree means finding a temple, finding a bridge, finding a narrow place in the river; not every link in the chain necessarily survives, but tracing back layer by layer never hurts. The origins of temple-and-bridge culture are simple and blunt.
In Haining, Zhejiang, there is a Huiyuan Nunnery dedicated to Lord Guan (Guandi). The legend of Guan Yu flooding the seven armies with water is famous far and wide, so it is hardly strange that he could become a god who governs water. The Dabei Nunnery beside Yangjia Bridge here in Shijiabang may also be connected with this. If so, the great-compassionate martial god really does take on a touch of black humor—a kind of physical salvation.
On the western side of Yangjia Bridge, a Wukang stone bridge-center slab / dragon-gate stone is built into the steps; some sources say it may be a relic of Dabei Nunnery. The main body of Yangjia Bridge is mostly Jinshan stone, but judging by the bluestone masonry on the bridge abutments at both ends, it must have a long history and have been rebuilt many times; this carved Wukang stone slab may well be an original component of Yangjia Bridge. This ginkgo is called a "thousand-year ginkgo" in some sources; taking the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees as authoritative, it is 125 years old—yet it is indeed more splendid than many ginkgos that have been listed as 500 years old.

Usually, when we discuss a particular ginkgo, we have to trace it back to its roots. The records of Chongwu Temple in the old gazetteers are much the same, mostly recounting a history of several rises and several declines. But a turning point came with the 2004 edition of the Hengshan Town Gazetteer, which recorded the following story in written form:
"In Zhangjiagang Village there was a Granny Wu who had worked as a servant in Yuan Shikai's household. Once she followed her master to Mount Wutai to burn incense, and there met a monk who told her: this monk's patriarch, in order to fulfill the dying wish of a Yuan-dynasty Princess Baihua, had made a special trip to Wujiang and planted one ginkgo each at Pinging's Shusheng Temple, Shuangyang's Yongle Temple, and Sidu's Chongwu Temple."
The key phrase is plainly 'Princess Baihua,' and Princess Baihua is likewise a frequent figure in folk legend; from the very name we can glimpse the feelings of truth, goodness, and beauty that people have invested in her.
For example, in Changfeng County, Hefei, Anhui, there is a Tomb of Princess Baihua. Legend says that to guard the tomb and protect the mausoleum she built a temple beside the tomb of the King of Wu, and that out of loyalty to her ruler and love for her father she later left a dying wish to be buried there herself. But this Princess Baihua was the youngest daughter of Yang Xingmi, King of Wu during the Yang Wu period, which clearly does not match the Yuan-dynasty setting of the Wujiang legend.
And in Kunqu opera, four acts of Baihua Ji (Record of the Hundred Flowers) happen to survive. Its plot is said to be adapted from Ming-dynasty popular literature and roughly tells how during the Xuanhe reign of the Song, in the Fang La uprising, Fang La's sister, Princess Baihua, was a female general who led the rebel army bravely against the Song forces but was undone by the traitor Jiang Liuyun, and took her own life after defeat—a tragic and heroic tale. Although this again conflicts with the background of the ginkgo legend, Baihua Ji already contains many Suzhou traces, such as the siege of Dongting Mountain, and even an episode involving a mustering platform, which can echo the old gazetteers of Wujiang.
In the article 'The Ginkgo Trees of Wujiang,' published in the Jiangnan Times, the author holds that Princess Baihua was the daughter of a general who fought against the Jin; she formed a women's army and joined the fight against the Jin, and was named for the crown of a hundred flowers she wore. Unfortunately, no source for this version of the legend could be found, and this story undoubtedly still has its deviations.
In fact, among the old gazetteers of Suzhou itself, one can find only the record in the Daoguang Pinging Zhi: 'The mustering platform is at Dayu Weir; legend says it is the place where the Yuan Princess Baihua mustered her troops; it is now ruined.' This background at last satisfies the account in the 2004 Hengshan Town Gazetteer, and incidentally matches the episode of the female general reviewing her troops in Baihua Ji.
Since the legend in the 2004 Hengshan Town Gazetteer was itself formed relatively recently (as an oral account by Yuan Shikai's servant), may we not consider that this legend of tree-planting to fulfill Princess Baihua's dying wish was itself compounded from several legends: roughly inheriting the episode of the female general mustering troops from the Kunqu play Baihua Ji, and grafting on an ending like that of the legend in Changfeng County, Hefei, Anhui, of a dying wish to be buried alongside. And the three temples in the legend—Pinging's Shusheng Temple, Shuangyang's Yongle Temple, and Sidu's Chongwu Temple—are precisely three rather famous ancient-ginkgo viewing spots that survived in Wujiang into modern times. Although the ginkgo at Pinging's Shusheng Temple was destroyed in 1972, the Dashun Sauce Garden on its former site still produces 'Ginkgo Brand' chili oil and chili sauce.
In fact, we need not insist on the truth of the legend itself. In the great majority of cases, legends do not arise without cause; whether intentionally or not, the phenomenon itself directly or indirectly reflects the conceptions and subconscious of its subject, regardless of whether the phenomenon itself is right or wrong. Discussing and studying the process and causes of its formation is of benefit to the exploration of social history as a whole.

The towns southwest of Wujiang, such as Hengshan, form the dense core of the lou-and-gang waterway network on the southern shore of Lake Tai, long summed up in the saying 'thirty-six lou and seventy-two gang.' Where there is a harbor there are boats, and where there are boats there are naturally boat people. The predecessor of Baoben Temple at Tingzi Harbor was called Niangniang Temple (Goddess Temple), and two legends about it circulate locally. One holds that the 'Niangniang' is the Guanyin Bodhisattva invited from Mount Putuo; the other holds that the 'Niangniang' is the Mazu goddess invited by merchants from southern Fujian. Whether Putuo's Guanyin or southern Fujian's Mazu, both are unquestionably water-deity beliefs formed in coastal regions, strongly marked by the religious character of boat people; in some places where different cultures have interpenetrated deeply, the images of Guanyin and Mazu themselves even overlap to a certain degree.
Folk beliefs are often pluralistic in their early stages—vengeful ghosts and floating corpses, heroes and great men, and so on. As people in different regions (though these regions often share certain geographical conditions) gradually infused universal good wishes, deities of quite different origins began to be assigned similar functions, and in the end either became a school of their own through outstanding influence and won official recognition, or merged with other mainstream deities. Their own distinctive images gradually blurred over generations of oral transmission, leaving only a vague, distant title such as 'Lord,' 'General,' or 'Niangniang.' Seen this way, it is hardly surprising that Baoben Temple should possess two origin stories that are far apart yet exceptionally vague.

In Yinxing Village, Jinjiaba, there is a towering ginkgo. Though tall, it is not dense; only when the main trunk reaches one-third of its height does it suddenly burst out lateral branches in three directions. From a photograph alone its bulk cannot be felt; only standing beneath the tree does one marvel at its thickness.
Villagers say there was once a Jiqing Temple here, and in the narrow courtyard in front of the hall there were once two ancient ginkgos; one was unfortunately cut down because it affected the safety of the buildings. I could not find the Jiqing Temple described by the villagers in the old gazetteers. Although the Guangxu 'Continued Gazetteer of Wujiang County' (Qing dynasty, 1644–1912 CE) does mention a Jiqing Temple located at Nandouwei in Bachai, it is clearly a considerable geographical distance from this one.
But I believe there must once have been a hall of no small size here, and there must once have been the narrow courtyard in front of the hall that the villagers describe. From the branching pattern of the ginkgo it is not hard to imagine that it could scarcely stretch its body in the narrow space, and only began to spread its forks once it rose above the surrounding houses; but beside it there was another ancient ginkgo, so it could only grow in the other three directions.
The incense offerings here may have ceased; the villagers I asked could not even clearly remember which deity was enshrined in the temple. Yet every one of the villagers treasures this ancient tree as if it were a jewel: an elderly man spent his own money seeking experts to re-measure the tree's age (villagers currently claim the tree is 1,500 years old and no longer hang the ancient-tree plaque marked 700 years, but the new age has not received official recognition from the Wujiang Housing and Urban-Rural Development authorities); when the ancient tree fell ill, they raised funds among the village to find a doctor for it; and now everyone has renamed Hangtou Village as Yinxing Village, planted new ginkgos beside the ancient tree to keep it company, and built a brand-new Ginkgo Square.
Some information is recorded in writing, and must be carefully sifted; some memories are imprinted in the mind, and will grow blurred; some answers have their solution right in the riddle itself, and only lack someone to understand them.

The ancient tree at Donghe Chan Temple bears a plaque saying 1,400 years, while the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Famous Trees records 300 years; the volunteers who write tree steles and biographies joke that this is a fraud-grade overstatement. At Fuji Temple outside Changmen Gate in Gusu there was the custom of 'ya shenxian'—'ya' meaning to join the crowd and squeeze through people; a Wu-dialect proverb, 'ya naomang,' vividly depicts the sea of people at temple fairs. Legend says that on the 14th day of the fourth lunar month, the birthday of Lü Dongbin, he would descend to the mortal world disguised as a beggar, relieve suffering, write out divine prescriptions, and heal people's illnesses; this gradually evolved into a blessing-seeking activity.
Today's Donghe Chan Temple in Zhenhu Community of the Suzhou New District, though different legends circulate, has a similar activity: legend tells that the daughter of the Suzhou prefect fell ill and no doctor could cure her, until a local Zhenhu physician, Li Huaichun, cured her with acupuncture. Later, to commemorate the divine doctor, the villagers built Li Xianren Shrine, and every year on the 24th day of the seventh lunar month the people along the shores of Lake Tai would go to burn incense and pray for blessings—locally called 'ya xianren.'
One wonders whether it was influenced by the legendary Li Huaichun's good deeds; likewise for a daughter, the local prominent Zhang family, when marrying off a daughter, built three tea pavilions on the shores of Lake Tai to 'chongxi'—to dispel ill fortune with joyous celebration—and to convenience the local people. The Tongfu Tea Pavilion in front of Donghe Chan Temple is the only one remaining today. Beside the temple is the ginkgo; beneath the ginkgo is the tea pavilion; beside the tea pavilion is a landing; where does the landing lead? Naturally, to Tongfu ('reaching blessings'). The Zhang family's grand Xiande Hall has not survived, but through this tea pavilion—built without intending to—we remember this kind local worthy. We could not find Donghe Chan Temple in the old gazetteers, nor could we find Li Xianren Shrine; the truth of these legends is hard to verify, but the customs that have come down to today are beyond dispute. The ancient ginkgo in the courtyard, through more than three hundred years of passing time, still guards the residents of this native place.

The thousand-year ginkgo at Taiping Chan Temple is renowned throughout Suzhou, but the name "Taiping Chan Temple" itself does not have a long history. According to the Xiangcheng District Gazetteer, "Taiping Chan Temple" was originally the ancestral shrine of the Middle Sha branch of the Three Sha Wang family of the Southern Song (1127–1279 CE); at the end of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE) it was changed into the ancestral hall of Wang Guanshi Guisan; in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) it was used again as the Wang family nunnery Yongli Nunnery; and in the second year of the Yongzheng reign of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE; Yongzheng reigned 1723–1735), the front hall of the nunnery was rebuilt as a Mengjiang Hall, known locally in older times as the "Shang Tianwang Liu Chengzhong Temple"; only in recent years was it expanded into today's Taiping Chan Temple.

Although Liu Mengjiang is a "water people" (shuishang ren) belief widely spread along the shores of Lake Tai, it survives only sparsely in the northern part of Suzhou prefectural city, and such beliefs often share similar causes. Professor Zhao Shiyu holds that "water people" families of Dongting East Mountain often took advantage of wartime opportunities when the state redefined land rights to come ashore through means such as uxorilocal marriage, and after gaining a firm foothold they "manufactured" ancestral origins by compiling genealogies to gloss over the family's standing—for example, claiming that "our ancestor was a recluse who came south with the Song imperial house." Seen in this light, the claim by the Taiping Wang family to be "descendants of the Taiyuan Wang who moved south" seems to share something in common with this, and the conversion of the family nunnery into a Mengjiang Hall likewise shows the close connection between the Taiping Wang family and "water people" beliefs. Taiping Town is adjacent to the Yangcheng Lake basin, and the Mengjiang belief there, similar to that of the Lake Tai basin, may hint at the possible true identity of the Taiping Wang family's ancestors.

By coincidence, every year on the 28th day of the third lunar month, Taiping's Mengjiang Hall holds the "Shang Tianwang Liu Mengjiang Procession." This procession date is entirely different from those along the shores of Lake Tai, but it happens to fall on the birthday of the Eastern Peak (Dongyue); recently some scholars have proposed that Liu Mengjiang may be an auxiliary deity of the Eastern Peak, and the date may serve as mutual corroboration for this view. Although Liu Mengjiang is found everywhere in the Wu region, the belief takes various forms; even though Liu Mengjiang entered the official sacrificial register during the Yongzheng reign, this could only unify it in form, while the content in each township still has its own distinctive character. In-depth study of folk beliefs is an important component of completing the social history of a locality. And today, roughly updating the Mengjiang belief, which has been transmitted in an orderly sequence, into a universal faith represented by "Taiping Chan Temple" may still require further discussion.

Suzhou Industrial Park has only four ancient and notable trees, three of which are ginkgos; one of those ginkgos has died and been deregistered, so only the two ancient ginkgos described in this text remain. The villages where these two ancient trees stand were long ago demolished, yet at the gate of the water company—and even inside the construction site of the industrial park—traces of incense offerings can still be glimpsed. This shows that both trees were community trees (she shu) of village temples; even though the surroundings have been transformed beyond recognition, the believers of the original villages have not forgotten the coordinates of their old home.
Although they are registered under the park, the villages where they stand—Chaoqian Village and Wangbang Village—belonged to Wuzhong District until 2004, so in the Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees of Suzhou the prefixes of these two trees' numbers read directly 'Wuzhong' rather than 'Park.' In its early years the park's redevelopment was carried out on a remarkably bold scale; perhaps being transferred to park management relatively late was one of the reasons they unexpectedly survived.
If we spread out a map, we find ancient ginkgos scattered like stars across the junction of today's Suzhou Industrial Park, Wuzhong District and Wujiang District. Although describing this location today is inevitably long-winded, twenty years earlier we could simply have called it the 'Chefang area.' The ginkgos of Chaoqian and Wangbang villages also originally belonged to Chefang Town. Although experience tells us they were once village-temple trees, the events of 2004 have already grown dim, and it is hard to learn whom the incense that has continued to this day is offered to—and in another generation, perhaps even this folk custom, which looks somewhat out of place amid steel and concrete, will be hard to sustain.
The memory of Chefang Town is already distant, but through ancient trees one after another and old bridges one after another, it seems we can still piece together her outline here in 2024.

Yufeng Mountain in Tinglin Garden is to Kunshan what Tiger Hill is to Suzhou. The old Yufeng Mountain and Tiger Hill shared many similarities: the garden-like feel of a real mountain that seems artificial, concentrated clusters of shrines and tombs and of temples and monasteries, rich resources of ancient and notable trees, cliff inscriptions and traces of famous visitors... But the most similar thing was the immortal-hero air of a mountain hidden within a temple and ancient pagodas rising into the clouds.
The paired confrontation of the Lingxiao Pagoda of Huazang Temple and the Miaofeng Pagoda was once an iconic scenic site of Kunshan during the Republican period; regrettably, after the founding of the People's Republic, a radar station was built on Yufeng Mountain, and the two pagodas had to be demolished one after another. Yet according to the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees, the thousand-year-old ginkgo below Huazang Temple is classified as a relic of Huiju Temple—so where does this Huiju Temple here come from? According to the Gazetteer of Kunshan's Tinglin Garden, Huiju Temple was founded earlier, and Huazang Temple was once a subsidiary courtyard of Huiju Temple; in the Yuan dynasty Huiju Temple fell into disuse, and in the Ming dynasty Huazang Temple occupied the pagoda courtyard of Huiju Temple on Yufeng Mountain and was rebuilt there, while the site of Huiju Temple at the foot of Yufeng Mountain was used for the City God Temple. Today the site of Huazang Temple at the summit is still a radar station, and Huazang Temple has had to be rebuilt at the foot of the mountain. When the thousand-year-old ginkgo was planted, the foot of the mountain was still the mountain gate of Huiju Temple, and Huazang Temple had not yet risen to prominence; hence it is classified as a relic of Huiju Temple. Although Tinglin Garden today has lost the iconic landscape of the two pagodas facing each other, thanks to ancient sites such as the old ginkgo it remains a high ground of Kunshan's humanistic history.
In addition, at the entrance of Tinglin Garden's east gate, east of the Zhuanci Shrine of Gu Wenkang Gong, is a gathering place of nearly half of Kunshan's ancient and notable trees; the most famous of these should be a 310-year-old ancient qionghua viburnum, and the qionghua is precisely one of the Three Treasures of Kunshan famed throughout Jiangnan. Gu Wenkang Gong is Gu Dingchen; although the ancient city of Kunshan has a long history, it was not until the Yuan dynasty that rammed-earth walls were built, and during the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty Gu Dingchen began building brick-and-stone walls at Kunshan to guard against Japanese pirates—one could say that the present outline of the ancient city of Kunshan took shape in Gu Dingchen's time, and building a shrine in such a conspicuous place and maintaining it down to the present naturally reflects his important place in the history of Kunshan's urban construction.
Most of the ancient trees in Tinglin Garden are around 110 years old; this is because during his tenure Mr. Fang Huan, the first civil affairs chief of Kunshan County in the Republican period, vigorously promoted the modernization of Kunshan County and built a large amount of public infrastructure, and the modern park-style layout of Tinglin Garden today was gradually established during this period; Mr. Fang Huan's tomb is hidden among these ancient trees. From the founder of the old-era city of Kunshan to the opener of Kunshan's modernization in the new era, Tinglin Garden and Kunshan remember the city's worthies.
