Beside Qiyu Pond there is Qiyu Village, and in Qiyu Village there is Qiyu Temple. Where the name 'Qiyu' comes from, no documentary record remains; recently, perhaps to promote a simplified place name, a spelling 'Ze'o' has also appeared. For the ruined temples and monasteries of other towns in Kunshan, source material is rarely found; Qiyu Temple is different, and we can roughly sort out two versions.
Version one: Sun Quan's mother and Sun Shangxiang, on their way back to Suzhou, heard that worship at Qiyu Temple was efficacious; a eminent monk had foreseen this and had them plant a ginkgo tree, to pray for the fulfillment of Eastern Wu's great enterprise.
Version two: Sun Quan, Emperor of Eastern Wu, himself planted a ginkgo tree and personally ordered the building of Qiyu Temple, to seek the eternal endurance of Eastern Wu's realm and a lifespan longer than the ginkgo's.
Let us look at what the old gazetteers say. According to the Kunshan-Xinliang County Supplementary Gazetteer (Kun Xin Liang Xian Xu Xiu He Zhi), Qiyu Temple was originally named Fuyan Chan Temple, 'built by the monk Youshan in the first year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan'—and so the various wondrous tales that circulate collapse of themselves. I suspect these are a collection of stories passed down generation after generation in Qiyu Village, compiled and recorded when oral history was being done. As for exaggerated claims cited by officials, such as 'the First Ancient Monastery of Jiangnan' and 'one of only two and a half temples under heaven,' one can only laugh them off. This 1,700-year-old ginkgo is also often marketed as the 'King of Trees of Jiangsu,' when in fact Dongshan alone has a 2,000-year-old ginkgo; it is hard to understand where these bizarre claims came from. Though the stories are somewhat exaggerated, they do show the scale of Qiyu Temple in its day. According to the Dianshanhu Gazetteer: 'Qiyu Temple, billed as the First Temple under Heaven, drew pilgrims from near and far, and was especially thriving at each temple fair. On that day the temple grounds were filled with all kinds of food stalls, general merchandise stalls, and toy stalls, with goods of every description dazzling the eye. Pilgrims, fairgoers, and traders flocked to the temple grounds from all directions, a sea of people packed so tightly that not a drop could squeeze through.'
Today, in front of the ancient Qiyu ginkgo stands a tobacco-and-liquor supermarket; in winter old people often gather beside the tree to 'hatch in the sun.' Not far away, Qiyu Temple's Great Incense-Flower Bridge, 'Chongfu Bridge,' still spans the pond; though now hidden among the reed marshes and ignored by all, it can still be crossed, while the 'Small Incense-Flower Bridge' has been demolished and rebuilt as a modern highway bridge. In a sense, though Qiyu Temple no longer exists, the various benefits it brought to Qiyu Village continue to this day.

The name "Penglang" comes from "Penglai Langyuan" (the fairy gardens of Penglai), which shows how outstanding the people and spirit of this land have been. According to the Penglang Town Gazetteer, ancient ginkgos were very common in Penglang Town at that time, mostly distributed in front of temples and shrines. Yet today these two thousand-year-old ginkgos at the junction of Penglai Road and Pengqian Road are hard to identify; we tried asking local elders and, combining online materials with our own understanding alone, offer a simple reconstruction of their history.

In the Penglang town area there used to be one temple each in the south and the north, commonly called the South Temple and the North Temple. The South Temple was the City God Temple; who occupied the main seat is no longer known. It stood beside today's Penglai Road in the south of the town. In the late Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) the City God Temple newly established the "Pengxi Second-Class Primary School," commonly called the "foreign-style school"; during the Republic it was reorganized as the "Penglang Town National Central Primary School"; after Liberation it became "Kunshan County Penglang Middle School"; later the middle school moved out and the site was used for government offices. Now that the town area has been demolished, only these two thousand-year-old ginkgos remain, in an unowned, overgrown yard, but incense still burns outside the wall. Originally the City God Temple and the school coexisted, and through successive reconstructions the temple gradually withdrew from the stage of history. It is said that the teacher and student Hu Shiyu and Ye Shengtao once taught and learned from each other here, and these two thousand-year-old ginkgos may also have witnessed the growth of these Republican-era masters. The North Temple was the Jinli Nunnery, dedicated to the Three Officials (Sanguan) faith, located beside Taiping Bridge, also called Huanlong Bridge, in the north of the town; the "Jinli Evening Bell" was once one of the "Eight Scenes of Pengxi." In the late Qing a "Pengxi Public Primary School" was founded on the nunnery's original site, and thus Penglang Town acquired the curious distinction of calling its two primary schools the South Temple and the North Temple respectively. Today the original site has been rebuilt as the Sanguan Hall. There are now two towering ginkgos in the temple, but they are not ancient trees; according to Hu Shiyu's "Record of the Ancient Plum," the Jinli Nunnery once had two ancient plum trees. Today the ancient plums are gone, and Taiping Bridge has been repaired into disfigurement, so the old traces are hard to find.

According to the Zhangpu Town Gazetteer · Nangang Volume, this ginkgo in Tang Village is a relic of the village's "Yingzhen Daoist Abbey." The abbey was built in the mid-Chenghua era and was ultimately destroyed in the 1950s; its specific form is difficult to verify. Adding the "about 1476" mentioned in the town gazetteer to the tree age of "about 540 years" gives exactly 2016, while the plaque for the ancient and notable tree is dated 2017. From this it appears the ancient tree was dated through documentary sources.

This ancient ginkgo in Tang Village stands right beside the Xiaojing stream that runs through the village, close to a reinforced-concrete bridge. Beneath the tree is a small riverside landing, covered by the ginkgo. Perhaps we can divide "ancientness" into two kinds. The first is the "ancient" inherent in an ancient object itself—for example, construction methods peculiar to a certain period, traces of weathering and moss, marks of blows and damage, and so on. Defined this way, perhaps only this tree in Tang Village deserves to be called "ancient." The second is "ancient" in the fabric of the place: the temperament of Tang Village, where every household seems to pillow its head on the river, and the orderliness of houses arranged along the water, carrying a Jiangnan-specific "complexity"—perhaps this too can be called a "sense of life," a "sense of plainness." From this point of view, Tang Village is brimming with ancient charm. Unfortunately, after talking with the village elders, we learned that the old people of the village are growing old and the young are surging toward the new town; in the future the village will inevitably become quieter and emptier. Now seems to be the last window of opportunity for a visit. We seem to stand at just such a crossroads: even today, gathering oral accounts about the ancient tree is difficult—so how, in the future, can these seldom-visited corners continue to pass on their stories? And the riot of autumn leaves is precisely a tragic, heroic last radiance, burning up life to achieve the final glory before all things wither and flourish in turn. Gazing at the gradually slanting sunset in the distance, one sighs: is this not also a microcosm of the "Tang Villages" of the world?

Qinfeng Pagoda was built in the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), in 1008 CE. It was originally named for being close beside Qinzhu Hill, but most hills in Jiangnan were never as grand as their names suggest. By the eleventh year of the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), in 1746, villagers took earth to repair the Tongyu Community Granary and simply dug this little earthen mound away entirely. From then on, Qinfeng Pagoda itself became Qiandeng's Qinzhu.
The thousand-year ginkgo on the northwest side of the pagoda has a listed tree age of 1,010 years. The tree leans to the north, like a devout old man at worship; a friend, imitating Zijin Temple's phrasing, called it 'the ginkgo worshipping the Buddha.' Although from the ground the tree looks unremarkable, seen from the air its form is extraordinarily lively, like a rising golden auspicious cloud, as if a Dunhuang flying apsara had been expressed as a tree, or like a hairpin thrust into the bun of the petite, lovely town of Qiandeng. 'From the side it is a ridge, from the peak it is a summit'—yes, Qin 'Peak.' People today have the benefit of drones; the ancients would presumably have climbed Qinfeng Pagoda to admire the ginkgo. This tree has a temper of its own, refusing every angle from the pavilions and terraces near and far; only Qinfeng Pagoda alone can take in her beauty, and she and Qinfeng Pagoda seem to be one body. If we subtract the listed age of 1,010 years from the listing year of 2020, the result is exactly 1,010—almost the same lifespan as Qinfeng Pagoda. One pagoda and one tree nestled together for a thousand years: truly a fine tale.

In the southwest of Kunshan county town there is a series of incongruous place names: Xiyuan Street, Xisi Lane, Shichuang Lane. Needless to say, there must once have been a temple of no small scale here. According to the map in the Continued Revised Combined Gazetteer of Kunshan and Xin, this place was once marked 'West Temple'—that is, the renowned Jingde Teaching Temple of Kunshan's history. Though the Jingde Teaching Temple no longer exists, it has passed down the precious Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) manuscript edition of the Buddhist canon, the Kunshan County Jingde Temple Great Canon, now held in the Tianjin Museum.
According to modern historical sources, the Republican-era Kunshan County government built a public library on the old foundation of the Jingde Teaching Temple—today's 'Red Building,' the Hou Beiren Art Museum. And now, not far from the Red Building, in the car park of the Federation of Trade Unions, two century-old ginkgos are hidden; I think they too must have stood within the Jingde Teaching Temple's bounds in their day.
The origin of the Jingde Teaching Temple is not hard to explain; old gazetteers describe it in much the same way: in the second year of the Xianhe era of the Eastern Jin (327 CE), the local official Wang Min donated his residence to found Baoma Temple, and in the third year of the Jingde era of the Song (1006 CE) it was changed to its present name. Friends familiar with Suzhou place names may already feel a sense of déjà vu—does 'Jingde Road' near Guanqian seem to have a similar origin?
According to the Daoguang-era Suzhou Prefectural Gazetteer, the Shrine of Duke Wenke Wang (today's provincially protected Wang Ao Shrine) stands on the foundation of the old Jingde Temple, showing that there was indeed a Jingde Temple on Jingde Road at that time. The Republican-era Investigations of Song Pingjiang City Walls and Lanes gives a literature review of materials on Suzhou's Jingde Temple; though it cites several old gazetteers, there are no obvious contradictions, only differences in detail, from which we can obtain two important pieces of information: 1. The Jingde Temple was east of Huangniufang Bridge in the northwest of the county—Huangniufang Bridge being the name on the Southern Song (1127–1279 CE) Pingjiang Map, now called Huanglifang Bridge, which matches the present location of the Wang Ao Shrine. 2. The origin of the Jingde Temple is connected with the former residence of Wang Xun or his younger brother Wang Min; the Record of Wu Lands says 'in the second year of Xianhe of the Jin, Duke Xianmu Wang Xun's younger brother Min donated his residence to build it,' which is exactly the same as the record of Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple.
Content about the Jingde Temple first appears in the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE) Record of Wu Lands; in that old gazetteer both Suzhou's Jingde Temple and Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple were built in the second year of Xianhe of the Jin, and Suzhou's Jingde Temple was assigned the story of Wang Min donating his residence as a temple. However, much of the Record of Wu Lands has been lost, and Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple is already called Jingde Temple rather than Baoma Temple in the book, showing that this is content added after the third year of the Jingde era of the Song. And in Kunshan's earliest gazetteer, the Chunyou-era Yufeng Gazetteer of the Song (960–1279 CE), Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple is also recorded as founded in the second year of Xianhe of the Jin by Wang Min donating his residence, with the addition: 'Today the eastern side-hall of the temple has a Shrine of Prefect Wang. The prefect is Min.'
To sum up: Suzhou's Jingde Temple first laid claim to Wang Min's IP, while Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple has more supplementary detail, making it hard to judge which Jingde Temple it was whose residence was donated to become a temple.
At this point we are surely full of curiosity about Wang Min—could this old gentleman have gone around the world donating his residence to found temples, in the same year, with the temples happening to share the same name? Wang Min happens to be included in volume 65 of the Book of Jin; though his life is not covered in much detail, we can learn that he died in the thirteenth year of Taiyuan of the Jin (388 CE) at the age of 38, from which we can calculate that he was born in 351 CE. But the 'second year of Xianhe of the Jin' mentioned in several old gazetteers is 327 CE—how could he have donated his residence to found a temple before he was born? The Kunshan Daily article 'Wang Min and Jingde Temple,' published on 23 February 2011, also pointed out this problem, and found that among Kunshan's successive old gazetteers only the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) author omitted the year, perhaps having noticed the contradiction between Wang Min's life and the Jingde Teaching Temple's history, while the other old gazetteers basically continued the Yufeng Gazetteer's account.
But now both temples are destroyed, and this documentary farce seems to have sunk into the sea of history, its truth hard to find.

The ancient ginkgo in Fangta Garden is almost the same age as the Chongjiao Xingfu Temple Pagoda. Today the temple has vanished into history, and only the pagoda and the ginkgo remain. Looking at the square pagoda from Ta Nong, it is very much like a yellowed old photograph: the narrow strip of sky is full of tangled electric wires, and the pagoda labors to thrust itself out through the gaps, then stands tall. Considerately, it has kept watch over the heights of the surrounding garden buildings, not rising too far above them, and together with the ginkgo it forms a harmonious and elegant golden ratio—just like the Jiangnan of a painting.
Unlike the slender forms of other square pagodas in Jiangnan, the Guangfu Temple Pagoda is a brick-and-timber pagoda that combines the grace of the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) with the stately beauty of the High Tang (618–907 CE). Sitting on Yushan and with Shang Lake at its back, its unique geographical setting lets its flying eaves kiss the blue of water and sky as one, and share with the flocks of homing birds the clearest stretch of sky in Yucheng. The square pagoda seems to have become a symbol of Changshu: from the old cigarette packs that our fathers kept close at hand to the labels on the caps of yellow-rice-wine bottles on the dinner table, it is as if even the smoke rings breathed out by old Changshu people trace the outline of the square pagoda. It is like a pillar that anchors the sea: never mind how the great households beneath the pagoda come and go, so long as Shang Lake does not run dry and Yushan does not fall, and so long as the pagoda, screened by the ancient ginkgo, still lifts its eaves as it did when first built in the Song, Changshu will remain that ancient and beautiful Haiyu Qinchuan.

The Chinese trumpet vine fits the graduation season remarkably well: enterprising, always spreading upward; clean and crisp, with a simple flower shape that forever faces the sky; optimistic and passionate, with a highly saturated, healing warm palette that is never greasy, seeming to carry a touch of youthful spirit. Different from all this, this first-grade ancient Chinese trumpet vine in Yanyuan Garden, Changshu, is currently the oldest Chinese trumpet vine in the Suzhou area. It did not bloom together with the main body in June; now, as the height of summer draws to a close, it blooms brilliantly instead. It seems that whether people or plants, the old possess some unusual wisdom. The full bloom of the Chinese trumpet vine is a rare highlight of the year in Yanyuan Garden's North Garden, combining the elegance of a classical garden with the refinements of modern horticulture.
Drawing on some online sources, one may perhaps guess that it came from the demolished No. 1-1 Zhoushenmiao Lane. Volunteers for the Tree Monuments project visited Yanyuan Garden several times, and the garden's staff all said it was not an original of Yanyuan Garden. First, very few ancient Chinese trumpet vines survive; at present this is the only first-grade ancient tree of its kind in the Suzhou area. Second, in old photographs this ancient tree likewise leaned against a lake rock, so conditions for transplanting existed. Today, however, this lake rock may have been placed the wrong way round; the face displayed outward is not very attractive.
Considering that Chinese trumpet vines are very hard to keep alive when transplanted, it is understandable that this vine is now pruned in a not particularly attractive way; one might even call it lucky enough. Ji Xianlin's "The Tragedy of a Quiet Path" was once included in the Jiangsu Education Press junior-high Chinese textbook; it recounts the special experiences of a vine plant in Beijing's Yanyuan Garden in a special era, and is worth reading.

The Suzhou Ancient and Famous Trees Gazetteer records a total of three ancient white yulan magnolias from Changshu. The white yulan magnolia at Xingfu Temple has already died; the remaining two white yulan magnolias are hidden in the Zhi Garden at Changshu First People's Hospital. Chen Yinke's 'A Separate Biography of Liu Rushi' opens with an ode to the red bean: "In former years, while sojourning in Kunming, I happened to purchase a single red bean from the Qian family's old garden at Baimao Port in Changshu, and so I had the idea of annotating and explaining the poems on the bond between Qian and Liu." The residence of Qian Qianyi and Liu Rushi at Baimao had a century-old red-bean tree planted during the Jiajing reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), and people of the time called it "Hongdou Villa" (Red-bean Villa).
The red-bean tree's flowering and fruiting is a rare event, occurring perhaps once in several decades. In former times it drew literary men to write poems about it; today it attracts media attention, and almost every occasion leaves a written record. In the eighteenth year of the Shunzhi reign of the Qing dynasty (1661 CE), when Qian Qianyi was celebrating his eightieth birthday, "the red-bean tree flowered again after twenty years, and by the ninth day, at the time of my humble birthday, it had set just one seed," delighting the couple immensely; Qian Qianyi wrote eighteen red-bean poems in one burst. In the fourth year of the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty (1824 CE), the red-bean tree bloomed in full; Qu Shaoji and his son Qu Yong, owners of the Iron String and Copper Sword Pavilion (Tieqin Tongjian Lou), made a special trip to view it, and after returning asked friends to make a painting and inscribe poems, which were bound together as the 'Red-bean Flower Painting and Poetry Album'—entrusting their longing to ancients of a hundred years before, and leaving it for us a hundred years later.

These two Chinese catalpas stand outside the mountain gate of Sanfeng Temple and have almost become the emblem of Sanfeng Temple; they are one of only three places in greater Suzhou where ancient Chinese catalpa blossoms can be enjoyed. The Chinese catalpa may be counted a native tree planted everywhere in the north, but on coming to Jiangnan it has become a rare tree whose value lies in its scarcity.
Yet the Chinese catalpa blossom bears the character "qiu" (autumn), though it is by no means an autumn flower—how is this to be explained? If we exercise a little imagination and cut spring into three parts—early spring, mid-spring, and late spring—then add the Jiangnan early summer, whose profusion of blossoms rivals spring itself, we get four equal parts. The Chinese catalpa blooms in late spring, which happens to be the very end of the three springs, precisely the "autumn" of the four equal parts. The two Chinese catalpas at Sanfeng Temple are even more special: their flowering season seems to come a week later than that of other Chinese catalpas. Seen from a certain angle, they are exceedingly considerate: they do not trouble us when the hundred flowers vie in beauty, and when the blossoms are fading they silently bring a tree full of fragrance before us as consolation. Perhaps few mention them, but they are always here, blooming on time in the season when the fragrance is spent.

Baoyan bayberries are renowned throughout Jiangnan. According to the Kangxi-era "Changshu County Gazetteer," "in the fourth month, Baoyan bayberries are at their most abundant, and visitors go in groups to view them, an activity called 'looking at bayberries.'" Yet the listed ancient bayberry trees at Baoyan are not growing especially well. The oldest, 常543, died about eight years ago; its original site was the center of the roundabout in the middle of the uphill trail, and its root base has now been filled in. At the original site of 常540, one can find 常543's early blue tag; at that time Changshu's ancient and notable tree numbering had not yet been reorganized, so the number on the tag then was 常0044. The original sites of 常538, 常539, and 常540 were all on either side of the uphill trail. Not long after 常543 died, these three trees underwent the reorganization of ancient and notable tree numbering; in that assessment, their ages were all adjusted from the original 120 years to the present 315 years. According to the recollection of an uncle who runs a tea room in the scenic area, after the previous round of renovations at Baoyan Scenic Area, the scenic area seems to have transplanted 常540 to the plaza on the south side of the scenic-area entrance, while at 常540's original site they placed 常543's early blue tag as a marker.
In fact, within the tea rooms and bayberry orchards contracted by farming households inside Baoyan Scenic Area, there are many unlisted old trees whose size and growth are far better than those of these few listed ancient trees; the farmers say orally that these trees are all over a hundred years old. Because fruit trees are economic crops, privately contracted ancient trees often receive more meticulous care than ordinary ancient and notable trees.

Beside Jijia Bridge stands an ancient ginkgo, and beside the ancient ginkgo there was once an old temple. According to the villagers, it was originally the Sanyuan Ci (Shrine of the Three Officials); in recent years some scholars have also suggested it may have been a shrine to Zhou the God (Zhou the Filial Son). Zhou Rong (Zhou the God / Zhou the Filial Son) is a local deity of Changshu who was elevated to divine status; in life he practiced the filial piety taught by Yan Yan, the "Confucius of the South": for his mother, who suffered from an eye ailment, he "licked [her eyes] until her sight returned," and for his gravely ill father he "scraped flesh from his thigh to make a broth and offered it to him." The people of Changshu admired him and built a temple in his memory after his death; the old gazetteers also record many instances of him displaying miracles and saving people from fire and flood. Temples dedicated to him are therefore widespread in the Changshu area, and around most of these temples there are also ancient ginkgos—perhaps somewhat in the manner of the Mengjiang Hall at Dongshan.

Local villagers say that every year many villagers who have moved away return to visit this ancient ginkgo. Many are folk who lived in the village as children and later settled in the city; some even come back specially from Shanghai. Though ordinarily scattered far and wide, each late autumn they seem, touched by the spirit of "Zhou the Filial Son," to gather in their old home without prior arrangement.

Standing beneath the tree, it seems even the sunlight takes on its warm yellow hue; a flood of gold pours down with the light, laying a dignified and splendid golden dress over the aged stone-slab bridge, and paving a golden road home for those who feel timid about nearing their native place—such is the charm of a village tree. However long we have been away, however far from home, we are forever certain that it will be waiting for us beside that bridge we have crossed countless times.

Taicang has a little-known garden called Dongting Fenxiu Garden, whose recent history has been fairly complicated. It was originally a small pleasure garden within Taicang No. 1 Middle School, and successively became the archaeological excavation site of the Fancun Jing site and then the construction site of the Dongting Fenxiu Yayuan residential development. Because its location has always made it hard for outsiders to see, it is somewhat awkward despite its outstanding cultural and historical status. The No. 1 Middle School campus was once the site of the Taicang Prefectural Examination Hall in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE); originally, north of the wisteria trellis stood an examination hall stele inscribed by Lu Zengxiang, of considerable historiographical value, which has now been moved to the school's new campus. For many people, the first question upon entering Shuangxing Temple is: why does "Shuangxing" (Double Ginkgo) Temple have three ancient ginkgos? According to the Zhangjiagang Archives, Shuangxing Temple was originally a River God Temple; when it was expanded, the monks planted two ginkgos by hand, and only then was it renamed Shuangxing Temple. Several decades later another was planted to make up the number, creating today's arrangement of three ginkgos. In sharp contrast to the strictly disciplined Shuangxing Temple, the street beside it is the busiest commercial quarter of the old Nianfeng town area. "Humans and gods rejoicing together" seems a more fitting description: in the villages of Jiangnan in former times, temples and shrines often became subtle public spaces, with something of the feel of a council chamber or a great hall. Places with temples are often the liveliest; commerce thrives on foot traffic, and temples need supplies—the two hit it off at once, and the pairing of temple and market quickly became an established and solid social consensus.
The people setting up stalls on old Nianfeng Street are all local grandpas and grandmas; you could say they are doing business, but really they just want to find old friends to chat about family matters and pass the time. In the clear green canal, flecks of white light glimmer; on the bank, an old man in a rattan chair gently waves a palm-leaf fan, and on the ground within reach of his fingertips an old radio sings opera as if no one else were around. My eyes wandered, and I stumbled by mistake into an old barbershop with yellowing wallpaper; the scissors in hand went "snip, snip, snip" like a dancing butterfly, flying together with the ginkgo leaves filling the sky toward a long, distant old time. As for whether the incense at Shuangxing Temple is truly efficacious, people look at these three ancient ginkgos that have weathered every calamity and still stand tall, and in their hearts they have long since made up their minds.

About the Dongshan Carved Building: the Dongshan Carved Building is an important residence-garden in the Wuzhong area, divisible into the Ming-dynasty (1368–1644 CE) hall Qinde Tang and the Republican-era (1912–1949) storeyed hall Chunzai Lou, the latter added by expanding northward from the former. What we know today as the Dongshan Carved Building usually refers to Chunzai Lou, but Qinde Tang, as a relatively well-preserved Ming hall with a comparatively early recorded date in Suzhou, is also an indispensable component; some ancient and notable trees, such as Buddhist pine, purple nanmu and wintersweet, are also distributed around Qinde Tang.
Chunzai Lou faces east and takes its name from the phrase "a sunny household enjoys spring forever." It consists of four parts: the brick-carved gatehouse, the front building, the rear building and the garden. The whole building makes extensive use of traditional auspicious patterns and opera-story carvings, while also employing Western architectural elements such as Corinthian columns, cast-iron railings and stained glass. Interestingly, the Ming Changwu Zhi (Treatise on Superfluous Things) holds that "three-storey high pavilions are the most vulgar," and storeyed halls in the Wuzhong area are mostly of two storeys, yet the rear building of Chunzai Lou chose a double-eaved three-storey form. Beyond the family's outstanding economic strength, this also reflects an open-minded attitude willing to break through dogma, and these architectural features in turn influenced the layout of the garden.
The Chunzai Lou garden lies in the narrow, elongated space north of the storeyed hall, running laterally across the brick-carved gatehouse, front building and rear building, serving a connecting role similar to a service passage. Because it is enclosed east and west by tall buildings and walls and is extremely narrow north to south, the choice of garden vegetation is quite bold: tall trees are densely planted—Chinese juniper, crape myrtle, Hai'er Lian camellia, banana shrub and others—while low plantings of wintersweet, nandina and the like provide accents. To enrich the layers of scenery and enhance three-dimensional depth in the cramped garden, galleries were built on the upper floors and pavilions topped with upper storeys, so that high buildings lean on tall trees and one can pluck the stars by hand; below, long pools are bridged to extend the water and rockeries rise against the walls, so that low scenery faces low trees and the foot can tread the cosmos. Together these ultimately form the garden with the highest density of ancient and notable trees in Wuzhong District.
